description: Comprehensive question bank derived from Earth.pdf covering all sections: Origin and Evolution, Theories, Age, Shape and Geoid, Size and Dimensions, Land and Water Distribution, Hemispheres, Important Parallels, Great and Small Circles, Latitude, Longitude, Quick Reference, Exam Traps, and Numerical Facts. Designed for KEA examination preparation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is Earth's position from the Sun?

options.A: First planet

questions.explanation: Earth is the third planet from the Sun.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which planet is presently known to support life?

options.A: Mars

questions.explanation: Earth is the only planet presently known to support life.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What type of planet is Earth?

options.A: Gas giant

questions.explanation: Earth is a terrestrial (rocky) planet with a solid surface.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: When did Earth begin to form?

options.A: About 4.54 billion years ago

questions.explanation: Earth began forming about 4.54 billion years ago from material in the early Solar System.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: According to the modern scientific explanation, how did Earth form?

options.A: By a giant impact with another planet
options.B: By accretion of dust and small rocky and metallic bodies
options.C: By condensation of a passing star's material
options.D: By volcanic eruption from the Sun

questions.explanation: Earth formed by accretion: dust and small rocky and metallic bodies in the solar nebula collided and gradually combined under gravity.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is accretion in planetary formation?

options.A: The gradual growth of a body as smaller particles and bodies collide and stick together
options.B: The splitting of a large body into smaller pieces
options.C: The melting of a planet's core
options.D: The evaporation of gases from a planet

questions.explanation: Accretion is the gradual growth of a body as smaller particles and bodies collide and stick together under gravitational attraction and other physical forces.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What was the early Earth like?

options.A: Cold and icy
options.B: Extremely hot with much material molten or partially molten

questions.explanation: The early Earth was extremely hot because of accretion impacts, gravitational compression and radioactive decay; much of its material was molten or partially molten.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is planetary differentiation?

options.A: The process by which dense materials sank towards Earth's centre while lighter materials rose
options.B: The process of continents drifting apart
options.C: The formation of the atmosphere from volcanic gases
options.D: The cooling of Earth's surface to form a crust

questions.explanation: Planetary differentiation is the process by which dense materials, especially iron and nickel, sank towards Earth's centre while lighter silicate materials rose, helping form the core, mantle and crust.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How did Earth's early atmosphere develop?

options.A: Through photosynthesis by plants
options.B: Largely through volcanic outgassing and release of gases from the interior
options.C: By capture of gases from the solar wind

questions.explanation: Earth's early atmosphere developed largely through volcanic outgassing and the release of gases from the interior; its composition changed over geological time.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How did Earth's oceans form?

options.A: Water vapour in the atmosphere condensed and contributed to rainfall; water was also supplied by water-bearing materials
options.B: Oceans formed from molten rock directly
options.C: Oceans were created by meteorite impacts only
options.D: Oceans formed from the Sun's heat

questions.explanation: As Earth cooled, water vapour in the atmosphere condensed and contributed to rainfall and the formation of early oceans; water was also supplied or supplemented by water-bearing materials delivered during the early history of the Solar System.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the approximate age of the oldest evidence of life on Earth?

options.A: At least about 3.5 billion years ago
options.B: At least about 4.54 billion years ago
options.C: At least about 2 billion years ago
options.D: At least about 1 billion years ago

questions.explanation: Evidence for life dates to at least about 3.5 billion years ago, although the precise timing and interpretation of the earliest evidence remain subjects of scientific research.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between the origin of Earth and the origin of the universe?

options.A: They are the same event
options.B: The origin of the universe concerns the beginning and expansion of the universe, while the origin of Earth concerns the later formation of our planet within the Solar System
options.C: The origin of Earth occurred before the origin of the universe
options.D: The origin of the universe concerns only the Solar System

questions.explanation: The origin of the universe concerns the beginning and expansion of the universe, while the origin of Earth concerns the later formation of our planet within the Solar System about 4.54 billion years ago.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the broad sequence of Earth's early formation?

options.A: Formation of gas-and-dust disk; accretion of planetesimals; growth of proto-Earth; heating and melting; core formation and differentiation; cooling and crust formation; development of oceans and atmosphere; later evolution of continents and life
options.B: Formation of oceans; accretion of planetesimals; core formation; development of atmosphere; evolution of life; formation of continents
options.C: Big Bang; formation of Sun; accretion of Earth; development of atmosphere; formation of oceans; evolution of life
options.D: Core formation; accretion of planetesimals; formation of gas-and-dust disk; cooling and crust formation; development of oceans

questions.explanation: A useful simplified sequence is: formation of the Solar System's gas-and-dust disk; accretion of planetesimals; growth of the proto-Earth; heating and melting; core formation and differentiation; cooling and crust formation; development of oceans and atmosphere; and later evolution of continents and life.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What are the major historical hypotheses traditionally discussed for the origin of the Earth and Solar System?

options.A: Nebular Hypothesis, Planetesimal Hypothesis and Tidal Hypothesis
options.B: Big Bang Theory, Steady State Theory and Oscillating Universe Theory
options.C: Plate Tectonics, Continental Drift and Seafloor Spreading

questions.explanation: The commonly taught historical hypotheses include the Nebular Hypothesis, Planetesimal Hypothesis and Tidal Hypothesis; modern science explains Solar System formation through a refined solar-nebula and accretion model.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What is the Nebular Hypothesis?

options.A: The Sun and planets originated from a rotating cloud of gas and dust that contracted under gravity
options.B: A passing star drew material from the Sun to form planets
options.C: A massive star passed close to the Sun and raised tidal forces
options.D: The universe began from a hot, dense state

questions.explanation: The Nebular Hypothesis proposes that the Sun and planets originated from a rotating cloud of gas and dust (a nebula) that contracted under gravity and formed the Solar System.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: Who first proposed an early nebular or gaseous hypothesis in 1755?

options.A: Immanuel Kant

questions.explanation: The German philosopher Immanuel Kant proposed an early version of the gaseous or nebular hypothesis in 1755.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: Who revised the Nebular Hypothesis in 1796?

options.A: Immanuel Kant

questions.explanation: The French mathematician and astronomer Pierre-Simon Laplace revised the nebular hypothesis in 1796.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What did Laplace's classical Nebular Hypothesis suggest?

options.A: A rotating, contracting gaseous nebula formed the Sun at its centre and shed rings of material from which planets gradually condensed
options.B: A passing star drew material from the Sun to form planetesimals
options.C: A massive star raised tidal forces that pulled out solar material
options.D: The universe began from a singularity

questions.explanation: Laplace proposed that a rotating, contracting gaseous nebula formed the Sun at its centre and shed rings of material from which planets gradually condensed.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What is the modern Solar Nebula Theory?

options.A: The Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago when a rotating cloud of gas and dust collapsed under gravity, forming the young Sun and a flattened protoplanetary disk
options.B: The Solar System formed from a passing star's material
options.C: The Solar System formed from tidal forces of a massive star
options.D: The Solar System formed from the Big Bang directly

questions.explanation: The modern Solar Nebula Theory states that the Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago when a rotating cloud of gas and dust collapsed under gravity, forming the young Sun and a flattened protoplanetary disk from which planets grew by accretion.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What is a protoplanetary disk?

options.A: A rotating disk of gas and dust surrounding a young star, within which planets can form
options.B: A disk of stars around a galaxy
options.C: A ring of asteroids around a planet
options.D: A layer of the Sun's atmosphere

questions.explanation: A protoplanetary disk is a rotating disk of gas and dust surrounding a young star, within which planets can form.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What is the Planetesimal Hypothesis?

options.A: A passing star drew material from the Sun through gravitational attraction; the material cooled into small solid bodies called planetesimals, which later combined to form planets
options.B: A rotating cloud of gas and dust contracted to form the Sun and planets
options.C: A massive star passed close to the Sun and raised tidal forces
options.D: The universe expanded from a hot, dense state

questions.explanation: The Planetesimal Hypothesis proposed that a passing star drew material from the Sun through gravitational attraction; the material cooled into small solid bodies called planetesimals, which later combined to form planets.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: Who proposed the Planetesimal Hypothesis?

options.A: Thomas C. Chamberlin and Forest R. Moulton

questions.explanation: The American scientists Thomas C. Chamberlin and Forest R. Moulton developed the Planetesimal Hypothesis in the early twentieth century, commonly dated to 1904.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What is a planetesimal?

options.A: A small solid body formed from dust and rock in the early Solar System that can collide and accrete with other bodies to build planets
options.D: A star in the early universe

questions.explanation: A planetesimal is a small solid body formed from dust and rock in the early Solar System that can collide and accrete with other bodies to build planets.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What is the Tidal Hypothesis?

options.A: A massive star passed close to the Sun and raised enormous tidal forces that pulled out solar material, which cooled and condensed into bodies that formed planets
options.B: A rotating cloud of gas and dust contracted to form the Sun and planets
options.C: A passing star drew material from the Sun to form planetesimals
options.D: The universe began from a hot, dense state

questions.explanation: The Tidal Hypothesis proposed that a massive star passed close to the Sun and raised enormous tidal forces that pulled out solar material; this material was thought to cool and condense into bodies that formed planets.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: Who proposed the Tidal Hypothesis?

options.A: James Jeans and Harold Jeffreys
options.B: Thomas C. Chamberlin and Forest R. Moulton

questions.explanation: The British scientists James Jeans and Harold Jeffreys are associated with the Tidal Hypothesis, developed in the early twentieth century; Jeans presented a version in 1917-1919 and Jeffreys later modified and discussed it.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What is the main difference between the Planetesimal Hypothesis and the Tidal Hypothesis?

options.A: The Planetesimal Hypothesis emphasises the formation and accumulation of small solid planetesimals, whereas the Tidal Hypothesis emphasises long streams or filaments of material pulled from the Sun by tidal forces
options.B: The Planetesimal Hypothesis involves a rotating nebula, whereas the Tidal Hypothesis involves a passing star
options.C: The Planetesimal Hypothesis was proposed by Jeans, whereas the Tidal Hypothesis was proposed by Chamberlin
options.D: The Planetesimal Hypothesis explains the origin of the universe, whereas the Tidal Hypothesis explains the origin of Earth

questions.explanation: Both historical hypotheses involve a close stellar encounter, but the Planetesimal Hypothesis emphasises the formation and accumulation of small solid planetesimals, whereas the Tidal Hypothesis emphasises long streams or filaments of material pulled from the Sun by tidal forces.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What is the main limitation of the classical passing-star hypotheses?

options.A: They do not adequately explain the observed angular-momentum distribution and the physical conditions needed to form the planets
options.B: They cannot explain the existence of the Sun
options.C: They do not account for the age of the universe
options.D: They ignore the role of gravity

questions.explanation: They do not adequately explain the observed angular-momentum distribution and the physical conditions needed to form the planets; modern observations and models instead support formation within a protoplanetary disk.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: Which historical hypothesis is closest in broad outline to the accepted modern explanation?

options.A: The nebular family of ideas

questions.explanation: The nebular family of ideas is closest in broad outline, but the accepted modern explanation is a substantially revised solar-nebula model involving a disk, dust growth, planetesimals and accretion.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What is the Big Bang Theory?

options.A: The leading scientific model explaining the evolution of the universe from an extremely hot, dense early state, followed by expansion and cooling
options.B: The theory explaining the formation of Earth from a passing star
options.C: The theory explaining the origin of the Solar System from a nebula
options.D: The theory explaining the formation of continents

questions.explanation: The Big Bang Theory is the leading scientific model explaining the evolution of the universe from an extremely hot, dense early state, followed by expansion and cooling.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: Does the Big Bang Theory explain the direct formation of Earth?

options.A: Yes, it explains Earth's formation directly
options.B: No, it explains the evolution of the universe; Earth formed billions of years later from material in the Solar System
options.C: Yes, it explains both the universe and Earth's formation
options.D: No, it explains only the formation of the Sun

questions.explanation: No. The Big Bang Theory explains the evolution of the universe. Earth formed billions of years later from material in the Solar System.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: Approximately when did the Big Bang occur?

options.A: About 13.8 billion years ago

questions.explanation: The universe began its expansion about 13.8 billion years ago according to current scientific estimates.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What is the relationship between the Big Bang and the formation of Earth?

options.A: The Big Bang produced the early universe; stars later formed and created heavier elements; much later, about 4.54 billion years ago, the Sun and planets formed from a gas-and-dust cloud enriched by earlier generations of stars
options.B: The Big Bang directly created Earth at the same time
options.C: The Big Bang occurred after Earth formed
options.D: The Big Bang created the Sun but not Earth

questions.explanation: The Big Bang produced the early universe, while stars later formed and created many heavier elements; much later, about 4.54 billion years ago, the Sun and planets formed from a gas-and-dust cloud enriched by earlier generations of stars.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What is the difference between the age of the universe and the age of Earth?

options.A: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, whereas Earth is about 4.54 billion years old
options.B: The universe is about 4.54 billion years old, whereas Earth is about 13.8 billion years old
options.C: Both are about 13.8 billion years old
options.D: Both are about 4.54 billion years old

questions.explanation: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, whereas Earth is about 4.54 billion years old.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What is the expanding-universe concept?

options.A: Space itself expands, so on large scales distant galaxies are generally observed to move away from one another
options.B: The universe is static and unchanging
options.C: The universe is contracting towards a single point
options.D: Only the Solar System is expanding

questions.explanation: The expanding-universe concept states that space itself expands, so on large scales distant galaxies are generally observed to move away from one another.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: What is one major observational evidence supporting the Big Bang model?

options.A: The cosmic microwave background radiation
options.B: The existence of the Solar System
options.C: The presence of oceans on Earth

questions.explanation: The cosmic microwave background radiation, the redshift of distant galaxies and the observed abundance of light elements are major lines of evidence supporting the Big Bang model.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.chapter: Theories Regarding the Origin of Earth
questions.question: Who discovered the cosmic microwave background radiation in 1965?

options.A: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson
options.C: Thomas C. Chamberlin and Forest R. Moulton

questions.explanation: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson detected the cosmic microwave background radiation in 1965.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the accepted scientific age of Earth?

options.A: Approximately 4.54 billion years old

questions.explanation: Earth is approximately 4.54 billion years old, commonly rounded to 4.6 billion years in school-level textbooks.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How is the age of Earth estimated?

options.A: Mainly through radiometric dating of meteorites and ancient terrestrial and lunar materials
options.B: By counting the number of rock layers
options.C: By measuring the distance from the Sun
options.D: By studying the motion of galaxies

questions.explanation: Scientists estimate Earth's age mainly through radiometric dating of meteorites and ancient terrestrial and lunar materials, using radioactive isotope decay systems such as uranium-lead dating.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is radiometric dating?

options.A: A method of determining the age of rocks or minerals by measuring the proportions of radioactive parent isotopes and their stable daughter products
options.B: A method of measuring the distance to stars
options.C: A method of measuring Earth's gravitational field
options.D: A method of studying seismic waves

questions.explanation: Radiometric dating is a method of determining the age of rocks or minerals by measuring the proportions of radioactive parent isotopes and their stable daughter products.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why is the exact age of Earth not determined simply by dating its oldest rocks?

options.A: Earth's earliest crust has largely been recycled or altered by geological processes, so the oldest surviving rocks are younger than the planet itself
options.C: The oldest rocks are on the Moon
options.D: Earth's rocks are all the same age

questions.explanation: Earth's earliest crust has largely been recycled or altered by geological processes, so the oldest surviving rocks are younger than the planet itself.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the approximate age of the oldest known Earth minerals?

options.A: About 4.4 billion years old

questions.explanation: Some zircon crystals from Western Australia are about 4.4 billion years old, providing evidence that Earth's crust existed very early in its history.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does 4.54 billion years mean in millions of years?

options.A: 4,540 million years

questions.explanation: 4.54 billion years is equal to 4,540 million years.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.chapter: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.question: What is the general shape of Earth?

options.A: A perfect sphere
options.B: Approximately spherical but slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the Equator (oblate spheroid)

questions.explanation: Earth is approximately spherical but is slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the Equator; its reference geometric shape is commonly described as an oblate spheroid or oblate ellipsoid.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.chapter: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.question: Why is Earth not a perfect sphere?

options.A: Earth's rotation produces an equatorial bulge and polar flattening, while variations in topography and the gravity field make its actual figure more irregular
options.B: Earth was formed from a cube-shaped nebula
options.C: The Sun's gravity pulls Earth into an oval shape

questions.explanation: Earth's rotation produces an equatorial bulge and polar flattening, while variations in topography and the gravity field make its actual figure more irregular.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.chapter: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.question: What is an oblate spheroid?

options.A: A three-dimensional shape that is flattened at the poles and bulges around the Equator
options.C: A shape that is flattened at the Equator and bulges at the poles

questions.explanation: An oblate spheroid is a three-dimensional shape that is flattened at the poles and bulges around the Equator.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.chapter: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.question: What is the equatorial bulge?

options.A: The greater radius of Earth at the Equator compared with the radius from the centre to either pole, largely associated with Earth's rotation
options.B: The flattening of Earth at the Equator
options.C: The rise of mountains at the Equator
options.D: The expansion of the atmosphere at the Equator

questions.explanation: The equatorial bulge is the greater radius of Earth at the Equator compared with the radius from the centre to either pole, largely associated with Earth's rotation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.chapter: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.question: What is polar flattening?

options.A: The reduction in Earth's radius at the poles compared with its equatorial radius
options.B: The increase in Earth's radius at the poles
options.C: The flattening of mountains at the poles
options.D: The melting of ice at the poles

questions.explanation: Polar flattening is the reduction in Earth's radius at the poles compared with its equatorial radius.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.chapter: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.question: What is the geoid?

options.A: An irregular equipotential surface of Earth's gravity field that closely corresponds to mean sea level extended beneath the continents
options.C: The shape of Earth's solid crust only
options.D: The boundary between Earth's atmosphere and space

questions.explanation: The geoid is an irregular equipotential surface of Earth's gravity field that closely corresponds to mean sea level extended beneath the continents; it is used as a physical reference surface for measuring heights.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.chapter: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.question: Is the geoid a perfect mathematical shape?

options.A: Yes, it is a perfect sphere
options.B: No, it is irregular because Earth's gravity field varies from place to place due to differences in mass distribution
options.C: Yes, it is a perfect ellipsoid
options.D: No, it is a flat surface

questions.explanation: No. The geoid is irregular because Earth's gravity field varies from place to place due to differences in mass distribution inside and on the planet.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.chapter: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.question: What is the difference between a geoid and an ellipsoid?

options.A: An ellipsoid is a smooth mathematical reference shape used in geodesy, whereas the geoid is an irregular gravity-based reference surface that approximates mean sea level
options.B: A geoid is a mathematical shape, whereas an ellipsoid is a physical surface
options.D: An ellipsoid is irregular, whereas a geoid is smooth

questions.explanation: An ellipsoid is a smooth mathematical reference shape used in geodesy, whereas the geoid is an irregular gravity-based reference surface that approximates mean sea level.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.chapter: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.question: What is geodesy?

options.A: The science of measuring and monitoring Earth's shape, size, gravity field and the precise positions of points on its surface
options.B: The study of rocks and minerals
options.C: The study of stars and planets

questions.explanation: Geodesy is the science of measuring and monitoring Earth's shape, size, gravity field and the precise positions of points on its surface.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.chapter: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.question: Which is the longest radius of Earth?

options.A: Equatorial radius

questions.explanation: The equatorial radius is the longest radius, approximately 6,378.137 kilometres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.chapter: Shape of Earth and the Geoid
questions.question: Which is the shortest radius of Earth?

options.A: Equatorial radius

questions.explanation: The polar radius is the shortest radius, approximately 6,356.752 kilometres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: What is Earth's equatorial diameter?

options.A: Approximately 12,756 kilometres

questions.explanation: Earth's equatorial diameter is approximately 12,756 kilometres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: What is Earth's polar diameter?

options.A: Approximately 12,756 kilometres

questions.explanation: Earth's polar diameter is approximately 12,714 kilometres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: Why is Earth's equatorial diameter greater than its polar diameter?

options.A: Earth's rotation produces an equatorial bulge, making the equatorial diameter about 42 kilometres greater than the polar diameter
options.B: The Sun's gravity pulls Earth into an oval shape
options.C: The Moon's gravity distorts Earth's shape
options.D: Earth's atmosphere adds to the equatorial diameter

questions.explanation: Earth's rotation produces an equatorial bulge, making the equatorial diameter about 42 kilometres greater than the polar diameter.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: What is Earth's mean diameter approximately?

options.A: Approximately 12,742 kilometres

questions.explanation: Earth's mean diameter is approximately 12,742 kilometres; rounded school references may give about 12,700 or 12,750 kilometres depending on the convention used.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: What is Earth's equatorial radius?

options.A: Approximately 6,378.137 kilometres

questions.explanation: Earth's equatorial radius is approximately 6,378.137 kilometres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: What is Earth's polar radius?

options.A: Approximately 6,378.137 kilometres

questions.explanation: Earth's polar radius is approximately 6,356.752 kilometres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: What is Earth's mean radius approximately?

options.A: Approximately 6,371 kilometres

questions.explanation: Earth's mean radius is approximately 6,371 kilometres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: What is Earth's equatorial circumference?

options.A: Approximately 40,075 kilometres

questions.explanation: Earth's equatorial circumference is approximately 40,075 kilometres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: What is Earth's meridional or polar circumference approximately?

options.A: Approximately 40,075 kilometres

questions.explanation: The circumference measured around Earth through the poles is approximately 40,008 kilometres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: What is the total surface area of Earth?

options.A: Approximately 510.1 million square kilometres

questions.explanation: Earth's total surface area is approximately 510.1 million square kilometres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: What is the approximate area of Earth's water-covered surface?

options.A: Approximately 361.9 million square kilometres

questions.explanation: Water covers approximately 361.9 million square kilometres, or about 70.9 per cent of Earth's surface.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: What is the approximate area of Earth's land surface?

options.A: Approximately 148.9 million square kilometres

questions.explanation: Land covers approximately 148.9 million square kilometres, or about 29.1 per cent of Earth's surface.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: What is the difference between diameter and circumference?

options.A: Diameter is the straight-line distance through the centre from one side of a circle or sphere to the other, while circumference is the distance measured around the circle
options.B: Diameter is the distance around the circle, while circumference is the distance through the centre
options.D: Diameter applies only to spheres, while circumference applies only to circles

questions.explanation: Diameter is the straight-line distance through the centre from one side of a circle or sphere to the other, while circumference is the distance measured around the circle.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: What is the approximate mathematical relationship between a circle's circumference and diameter?

options.A: The circumference is π times its diameter; π is approximately 3.14159
options.B: The circumference is twice its diameter
options.C: The circumference is half its diameter
options.D: The circumference is equal to its diameter

questions.explanation: The circumference of a circle is π times its diameter; π is approximately 3.14159.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.topic: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.chapter: Size, Dimensions and Surface Area of Earth
questions.question: Which is greater, Earth's equatorial circumference or polar circumference?

options.A: Equatorial circumference

questions.explanation: Earth's equatorial circumference is greater because the equatorial radius is larger than the polar radius.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What percentage of Earth's surface is covered by water?

options.A: Approximately 71 per cent

questions.explanation: Approximately 71 per cent of Earth's surface is covered by water.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What percentage of Earth's surface is covered by land?

options.A: Approximately 29 per cent

questions.explanation: Approximately 29 per cent of Earth's surface is covered by land.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why is Earth called the Blue Planet?

options.A: Because oceans and other water bodies cover about 71 per cent of its surface and make it appear predominantly blue from space
options.D: Because it reflects blue light from the Sun

questions.explanation: Earth is called the Blue Planet because oceans and other water bodies cover about 71 per cent of its surface and make it appear predominantly blue from space.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?

options.A: Pacific Ocean

questions.explanation: The Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean on Earth.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which is the smallest ocean on Earth?

options.A: Arctic Ocean

questions.explanation: The Arctic Ocean is the smallest of the five recognised oceans.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which is the largest continent by area?

options.A: Asia

questions.explanation: Asia is the largest continent by area.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which is the smallest continent by area under the seven-continent model?

options.A: Australia

questions.explanation: Australia is the smallest continent under the commonly used seven-continent model.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Is most of Earth's water fresh water?

options.A: No, about 97 per cent of Earth's water is saline and only about 3 per cent is freshwater
options.B: Yes, about 97 per cent is freshwater
options.C: Yes, all of Earth's water is fresh
options.D: No, all of Earth's water is saline

questions.explanation: No. About 97 per cent of Earth's water is saline, mainly in oceans, and only about 3 per cent is freshwater; much of the freshwater is stored in glaciers, ice caps and groundwater.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the water hemisphere?

options.A: The half of Earth centred approximately in the South Pacific in which the greatest possible proportion of the surface is water
options.B: The half of Earth centred near western Europe

questions.explanation: The water hemisphere is the half of Earth centred approximately in the South Pacific in which the greatest possible proportion of the surface is water; it is not an official latitude-longitude hemisphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the land hemisphere?

options.A: The half of Earth centred approximately near western Europe in which the greatest possible proportion of land is concentrated
options.B: The half of Earth centred in the South Pacific

questions.explanation: The land hemisphere is the half of Earth centred approximately near western Europe in which the greatest possible proportion of land is concentrated; it is not identical to the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a hemisphere?

options.A: One half of a sphere or globe

questions.explanation: A hemisphere is one half of a sphere or globe.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres?

options.A: The Equator at 0° latitude

questions.explanation: The Equator at 0° latitude divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Northern Hemisphere?

options.A: The half of Earth located north of the Equator, extending from 0° to 90° N
options.B: The half of Earth located south of the Equator
options.C: The half of Earth between 0° and 180° east longitude
options.D: The half of Earth between 0° and 180° west longitude

questions.explanation: The Northern Hemisphere is the half of Earth located north of the Equator, extending from 0° to 90° N.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Southern Hemisphere?

options.A: The half of Earth located south of the Equator, extending from 0° to 90° S
options.B: The half of Earth located north of the Equator
options.C: The half of Earth between 0° and 180° east longitude
options.D: The half of Earth between 0° and 180° west longitude

questions.explanation: The Southern Hemisphere is the half of Earth located south of the Equator, extending from 0° to 90° S.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which hemisphere contains the greater proportion of Earth's land area?

options.A: Northern Hemisphere

questions.explanation: The Northern Hemisphere contains a greater proportion of Earth's land area than the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which hemisphere contains most of Earth's ocean area?

options.A: Southern Hemisphere

questions.explanation: The Southern Hemisphere contains a greater proportion of Earth's ocean area than the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which major continents lie wholly in the Northern Hemisphere?

options.A: Europe and North America

questions.explanation: Europe and North America lie wholly in the Northern Hemisphere; Asia is also wholly north of the Equator, while Africa and South America extend across the Equator.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which continent lies wholly in the Southern Hemisphere?

options.A: Antarctica

questions.explanation: Antarctica lies wholly in the Southern Hemisphere; Australia also lies wholly in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What divides Earth into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres in the conventional system?

options.A: The Prime Meridian at 0° longitude and the 180° meridian, taken together

questions.explanation: The Prime Meridian at 0° longitude and the 180° meridian, taken together, form the conventional division between the Eastern and Western Hemispheres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Eastern Hemisphere in the conventional division?

options.A: The half of Earth between 0° longitude and 180° east longitude
options.B: The half of Earth between 0° longitude and 180° west longitude
options.C: The half of Earth north of the Equator
options.D: The half of Earth south of the Equator

questions.explanation: In the conventional division, the Eastern Hemisphere is the half of Earth between 0° longitude and 180° east longitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Western Hemisphere in the conventional division?

options.A: The half of Earth between 0° longitude and 180° west longitude
options.B: The half of Earth between 0° longitude and 180° east longitude
options.C: The half of Earth north of the Equator
options.D: The half of Earth south of the Equator

questions.explanation: In the conventional division, the Western Hemisphere is the half of Earth between 0° longitude and 180° west longitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Is the Eastern-Western Hemisphere division uniquely fixed by nature?

options.A: No, unlike the Equator-based Northern and Southern division, the choice of the 0° and 180° meridians as the boundary is a conventional geographic reference
options.B: Yes, it is fixed by Earth's rotation
options.C: Yes, it is determined by the Sun's position
options.D: No, it is determined by the Moon's orbit

questions.explanation: No. Unlike the Equator-based Northern and Southern division, the choice of the 0° and 180° meridians as the boundary is a conventional geographic reference.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Equator?

options.A: The imaginary great circle at 0° latitude, equidistant from the North and South Poles, that divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres

questions.explanation: The Equator is the imaginary great circle at 0° latitude, equidistant from the North and South Poles, that divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the latitude of the Equator?
questions.explanation: The Equator is located at 0° latitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Tropic of Cancer?

options.A: The important parallel located approximately 23.5° north of the Equator; the overhead Sun reaches this latitude around the June solstice
options.B: The important parallel located approximately 23.5° south of the Equator
options.C: The important parallel located approximately 66.5° north of the Equator
options.D: The important parallel located at 0° latitude

questions.explanation: The Tropic of Cancer is the important parallel located approximately 23.5° north of the Equator; the overhead Sun reaches this latitude around the June solstice.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the latitude of the Tropic of Cancer?

options.A: Approximately 23°26' N, commonly rounded to 23.5° N
options.B: Approximately 23°26' S, commonly rounded to 23.5° S
options.C: Approximately 66°34' N, commonly rounded to 66.5° N

questions.explanation: The Tropic of Cancer is approximately 23°26' N, commonly rounded to 23.5° N.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Tropic of Capricorn?

options.A: The important parallel located approximately 23.5° south of the Equator; the overhead Sun reaches this latitude around the December solstice
options.B: The important parallel located approximately 23.5° north of the Equator
options.C: The important parallel located approximately 66.5° south of the Equator
options.D: The important parallel located at 0° latitude

questions.explanation: The Tropic of Capricorn is the important parallel located approximately 23.5° south of the Equator; the overhead Sun reaches this latitude around the December solstice.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the latitude of the Tropic of Capricorn?

options.A: Approximately 23°26' S, commonly rounded to 23.5° S
options.B: Approximately 23°26' N, commonly rounded to 23.5° N
options.C: Approximately 66°34' S, commonly rounded to 66.5° S

questions.explanation: The Tropic of Capricorn is approximately 23°26' S, commonly rounded to 23.5° S.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Arctic Circle?

options.A: The important parallel located approximately 66.5° north of the Equator and marks the southern limit of the Arctic polar day and polar night phenomena
options.B: The important parallel located approximately 66.5° south of the Equator
options.C: The important parallel located approximately 23.5° north of the Equator
options.D: The important parallel located at 0° latitude

questions.explanation: The Arctic Circle is the important parallel located approximately 66.5° north of the Equator and marks the southern limit of the Arctic polar day and polar night phenomena.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the latitude of the Arctic Circle?

options.A: Approximately 66°34' N, commonly rounded to 66.5° N
options.B: Approximately 66°34' S, commonly rounded to 66.5° S
options.C: Approximately 23°26' N, commonly rounded to 23.5° N

questions.explanation: The Arctic Circle is approximately 66°34' N, commonly rounded to 66.5° N.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Antarctic Circle?

options.A: The important parallel located approximately 66.5° south of the Equator and marks the northern limit of the Antarctic polar day and polar night phenomena
options.B: The important parallel located approximately 66.5° north of the Equator
options.C: The important parallel located approximately 23.5° south of the Equator
options.D: The important parallel located at 0° latitude

questions.explanation: The Antarctic Circle is the important parallel located approximately 66.5° south of the Equator and marks the northern limit of the Antarctic polar day and polar night phenomena.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the latitude of the Antarctic Circle?

options.A: Approximately 66°34' S, commonly rounded to 66.5° S
options.B: Approximately 66°34' N, commonly rounded to 66.5° N
options.C: Approximately 23°26' S, commonly rounded to 23.5° S

questions.explanation: The Antarctic Circle is approximately 66°34' S, commonly rounded to 66.5° S.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the latitude of the North Pole?
questions.explanation: The North Pole is located at 90° N latitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the latitude of the South Pole?
questions.explanation: The South Pole is located at 90° S latitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which five major parallels are most commonly identified on a globe?

options.A: Arctic Circle (66.5° N), Tropic of Cancer (23.5° N), Equator (0°), Tropic of Capricorn (23.5° S) and Antarctic Circle (66.5° S)
options.B: Prime Meridian (0°), 180° meridian, Arctic Circle, Tropic of Cancer, Tropic of Capricorn
options.C: North Pole (90° N), Arctic Circle (66.5° N), Equator (0°), Antarctic Circle (66.5° S), South Pole (90° S)
options.D: Tropic of Cancer (23.5° N), Equator (0°), Tropic of Capricorn (23.5° S), Prime Meridian (0°), 180° meridian

questions.explanation: The five major parallels are the Arctic Circle (66.5° N), Tropic of Cancer (23.5° N), Equator (0°), Tropic of Capricorn (23.5° S) and Antarctic Circle (66.5° S).

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which parallel is the longest on Earth?

options.A: The Equator

questions.explanation: The Equator is the longest parallel of latitude and is the only parallel that is a great circle.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which parallel receives the overhead Sun around 21 June?

options.A: The Tropic of Cancer

questions.explanation: The Tropic of Cancer receives the overhead midday Sun around the June solstice, usually on or about 21 June.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which parallel receives the overhead Sun around 22 December?

options.A: The Tropic of Capricorn

questions.explanation: The Tropic of Capricorn receives the overhead midday Sun around the December solstice, usually on or about 21 or 22 December.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the significance of the Arctic and Antarctic Circles?

options.A: They mark the approximate boundaries poleward of which at least one day each year can have continuous daylight and at least one day can have continuous darkness, due to Earth's axial tilt
options.B: They mark the boundaries of the Tropics

questions.explanation: They mark the approximate boundaries poleward of which at least one day each year can have continuous daylight and at least one day can have continuous darkness, due to Earth's axial tilt.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Torrid Zone?

options.A: The region between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, where the Sun can be directly overhead at noon at least once during the year
options.B: The region between the Arctic Circle and the North Pole
options.C: The region between the Antarctic Circle and the South Pole
options.D: The region between the Tropic of Cancer and the Arctic Circle

questions.explanation: The Torrid Zone is the region between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, where the Sun can be directly overhead at noon at least once during the year.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the Temperate Zones?

options.A: The zones that lie between the tropics and the polar circles in each hemisphere
options.B: The zones between the Arctic and Antarctic Circles
options.C: The zones between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn
options.D: The zones poleward of the polar circles

questions.explanation: The Temperate Zones lie between the tropics and the polar circles in each hemisphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the Frigid Zones?

options.A: The zones that lie between the Arctic Circle and the North Pole in the north, and between the Antarctic Circle and the South Pole in the south
options.C: The zones between the Tropics and the polar circles

questions.explanation: The Frigid Zones lie between the Arctic Circle and the North Pole in the north, and between the Antarctic Circle and the South Pole in the south.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a great circle?

options.A: A circle on a sphere whose plane passes through the centre of the sphere, dividing it into two equal hemispheres
options.B: A circle on a sphere whose plane does not pass through the centre
options.C: A circle that is parallel to the Equator
options.D: A circle that passes through the poles only

questions.explanation: A great circle is a circle on a sphere whose plane passes through the centre of the sphere, dividing it into two equal hemispheres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the most important example of a great circle on Earth?

options.A: The Equator

questions.explanation: The Equator is the most important parallel that is a great circle; every complete meridian paired with its opposite meridian also forms a great circle.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a small circle?

options.A: A circle on a sphere whose plane does not pass through the centre and which divides the sphere into two unequal parts
options.B: A circle on a sphere whose plane passes through the centre
options.C: A circle that divides the sphere into two equal hemispheres
options.D: A circle that passes through both poles

questions.explanation: A small circle is a circle on a sphere whose plane does not pass through the centre and which divides the sphere into two unequal parts.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Are all parallels of latitude great circles?

options.A: No, the Equator is the only parallel of latitude that is a great circle; all other parallels are small circles
options.B: Yes, all parallels are great circles
options.C: No, all parallels are small circles

questions.explanation: No. The Equator is the only parallel of latitude that is a great circle; all other parallels are small circles.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Are meridians of longitude great circles?

options.A: A single meridian is a semicircle from pole to pole; a meridian and its opposite meridian together form a great circle
options.B: Yes, every single meridian is a great circle
options.D: Only the Prime Meridian is a great circle

questions.explanation: A single meridian is a semicircle from pole to pole; a meridian and its opposite meridian together form a great circle.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why are great circles important in navigation?

options.A: The shortest route between two points on a sphere, measured along the surface, follows an arc of a great circle, which is why great-circle routes are important in long-distance navigation and aviation
options.B: They are the only circles that appear on maps
options.C: They are easier to draw than small circles
options.D: They divide Earth into equal hemispheres

questions.explanation: The shortest route between two points on a sphere, measured along the surface, follows an arc of a great circle, which is why great-circle routes are important in long-distance navigation and aviation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a meridian?

options.A: A line of longitude running from the North Pole to the South Pole
options.B: A line of latitude running east-west
options.C: A circle parallel to the Equator
options.D: A line that divides Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres

questions.explanation: A meridian is a line of longitude running from the North Pole to the South Pole.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a parallel?

options.A: A circle of latitude running east-west and joining all places that have the same latitude
options.B: A line of longitude running north-south
options.C: A line that passes through the poles
options.D: A line that divides Earth into Eastern and Western Hemispheres

questions.explanation: A parallel is a circle of latitude running east-west and joining all places that have the same latitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Do meridians meet?

options.A: Yes, all meridians converge at the North Pole and South Pole
options.C: Yes, they meet at the Equator

questions.explanation: Yes. All meridians converge at the North Pole and South Pole.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Do parallels meet?

options.A: No, parallels of latitude remain parallel to one another and do not meet, except that they shrink to points at the poles
options.B: Yes, they meet at the poles
options.C: Yes, they meet at the Equator
options.D: Yes, they meet at the Prime Meridian

questions.explanation: No. Parallels of latitude remain parallel to one another and do not meet, except that they shrink to points at the poles.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is latitude?

options.A: The angular distance of a place north or south of the Equator, measured at the centre of Earth along a meridian
options.B: The angular distance of a place east or west of the Prime Meridian
options.D: The height of a place above sea level

questions.explanation: Latitude is the angular distance of a place north or south of the Equator, measured at the centre of Earth along a meridian.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the range of latitude?

options.A: From 0° at the Equator to 90° N at the North Pole and 90° S at the South Pole

questions.explanation: Latitude ranges from 0° at the Equator to 90° N at the North Pole and 90° S at the South Pole.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In which units is latitude measured?

options.A: Degrees (°), minutes (') and seconds ("), or in decimal degrees

questions.explanation: Latitude is measured in degrees (°), minutes (') and seconds ("), or in decimal degrees.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How many degrees are there in a full circle of latitude measurement?

options.A: The angular measurement from the South Pole to the North Pole along a meridian is 180 degrees, comprising 90° north and 90° south of the Equator

questions.explanation: The angular measurement from the South Pole to the North Pole along a meridian is 180 degrees, comprising 90° north and 90° south of the Equator.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the approximate ground distance represented by one degree of latitude?

options.A: Approximately 111 kilometres

questions.explanation: One degree of latitude is approximately 111 kilometres, although the exact distance varies slightly with latitude because Earth is not a perfect sphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the approximate ground distance represented by one minute of latitude?

options.A: Approximately 1.85 kilometres, close to one nautical mile

questions.explanation: One minute of latitude is approximately 1.85 kilometres, close to one nautical mile.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the approximate ground distance represented by one second of latitude?

options.A: Approximately 31 metres

questions.explanation: One second of latitude is approximately 31 metres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Does the distance between adjacent parallels of latitude vary greatly?

options.A: No, the north-south ground distance between one-degree parallels is nearly constant, at about 111 kilometres, with small variations due to Earth's shape
options.B: Yes, it varies from 0 to 111 kilometres
options.C: Yes, it doubles towards the poles
options.D: Yes, it is greatest at the poles

questions.explanation: The north-south ground distance between one-degree parallels is nearly constant, at about 111 kilometres, with small variations due to Earth's shape.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the importance of latitude?

options.A: Latitude helps locate places north or south of the Equator and influences solar angle, day length, temperature patterns and broad climatic zones
options.C: Latitude determines the length of a year
options.D: Latitude determines the shape of Earth

questions.explanation: Latitude helps locate places north or south of the Equator and influences solar angle, day length, temperature patterns and broad climatic zones.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is longitude?

options.A: The angular distance of a place east or west of the Prime Meridian, measured in degrees along the Equator or an equivalent reference plane
options.B: The angular distance of a place north or south of the Equator
options.C: The height of a place above sea level

questions.explanation: Longitude is the angular distance of a place east or west of the Prime Meridian, measured in degrees along the Equator or an equivalent reference plane.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Prime Meridian?

options.A: The reference meridian at 0° longitude, passing through Greenwich in London, United Kingdom

questions.explanation: The Prime Meridian is the reference meridian at 0° longitude, passing through Greenwich in London, United Kingdom.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the range of longitude?

options.A: Longitude is measured from 0° to 180° east and from 0° to 180° west of the Prime Meridian

questions.explanation: Longitude is measured from 0° to 180° east and from 0° to 180° west of the Prime Meridian.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the 180° meridian?

options.A: The meridian opposite the Prime Meridian and forms the other half of the great circle through the 0° meridian

questions.explanation: The 180° meridian is the meridian opposite the Prime Meridian and forms the other half of the great circle through the 0° meridian.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the International Date Line?

options.A: A conventional, irregular line that follows roughly the 180° meridian and marks the place where the calendar date changes by one day when crossed
options.D: A line that divides Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres

questions.explanation: The International Date Line is a conventional, irregular line that follows roughly the 180° meridian and marks the place where the calendar date changes by one day when crossed.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Does the International Date Line follow the 180° meridian exactly?

options.A: No, it deviates from the 180° meridian in several places to avoid dividing countries and island groups into different calendar dates
options.B: Yes, it follows the 180° meridian exactly
options.C: No, it follows the Prime Meridian

questions.explanation: No. It deviates from the 180° meridian in several places to avoid dividing countries and island groups into different calendar dates.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the angular difference between successive meridians if the globe is divided into 360 equal degrees?

options.A: 1° of longitude

questions.explanation: The angular difference between successive whole-degree meridians is 1° of longitude.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does the ground distance represented by one degree of longitude vary with latitude?

options.A: It is greatest at the Equator, about 111 kilometres, and decreases towards the poles, becoming zero at the poles where all meridians meet
options.B: It is greatest at the poles and decreases towards the Equator
options.D: It is zero at the Equator and greatest at the poles

questions.explanation: It is greatest at the Equator, about 111 kilometres, and decreases towards the poles, becoming zero at the poles where all meridians meet.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the approximate time difference corresponding to 1° of longitude?

options.A: 4 minutes of local solar time

questions.explanation: One degree of longitude corresponds to 4 minutes of local solar time because Earth rotates through 360° in approximately 24 hours.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the time difference corresponding to 15° of longitude?

options.A: Approximately one hour of local solar time
options.B: Approximately 4 minutes of local solar time
options.C: Approximately 15 minutes of local solar time
options.D: Approximately 30 minutes of local solar time

questions.explanation: Fifteen degrees of longitude correspond to approximately one hour of local solar time.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the time difference corresponding to 1 minute of longitude?

options.A: 4 seconds of local solar time

questions.explanation: One minute of longitude corresponds to 4 seconds of local solar time.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why does longitude help determine time?

options.A: Earth rotates 360° in about 24 hours, so places at different longitudes experience local solar noon at different times; this relationship forms the basis of time zones
options.B: Longitude determines the length of a day

questions.explanation: Earth rotates 360° in about 24 hours, so places at different longitudes experience local solar noon at different times; this relationship forms the basis of time zones.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which meridian is used as the reference for Indian Standard Time?

options.A: 82°30' E meridian, which passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh

questions.explanation: Indian Standard Time is based on the 82°30' E meridian, which passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the time difference between Indian Standard Time and Greenwich Mean Time or UTC?

options.A: Indian Standard Time is UTC plus 5 hours 30 minutes
options.B: Indian Standard Time is UTC minus 5 hours 30 minutes
options.C: Indian Standard Time is UTC plus 4 hours
options.D: Indian Standard Time is UTC plus 6 hours

questions.explanation: Indian Standard Time is UTC plus 5 hours 30 minutes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between local time and standard time?

options.A: Local time is based on the Sun's apparent position at a particular longitude, while standard time is the uniform time adopted by a country or region for practical use
options.B: Local time is uniform across a country, while standard time varies with longitude
options.C: Local time is based on the Moon, while standard time is based on the Sun

questions.explanation: Local time is based on the Sun's apparent position at a particular longitude, while standard time is the uniform time adopted by a country or region for practical use.
